title: Verdant Systems - Escalation Postmortem Follow-up
summary: Follow-up on the incident on 2026-04-02 that caused elevated tail latency for inference in Verdant's Dedicated cluster. Reviewed root cause (KV cache thrash + autoscaler misconfiguration), mitigations deployed, and longer-term reliability improvements and runbook items. Agreed next steps: provide detailed logs & metrics, schedule a dedicated kernel-level benchmark, and add canary autoscaler rules.
next_steps: Redwood: share raw p99/p999 logs + autoscaler histograms by EOD 2026-04-09
Verdant: provide the exact workload replay traces and a prioritized list of critical routes by 2026-04-10
Schedule kernel/quantization benchmark session week of 2026-04-13
Joint runbook rewrite session scheduled for 2026-04-20
action_items: Michael Chen: upload debug logs and autoscaler snapshots to shared S3 bucket - due 2026-04-09
Sana Patel: run and share microbenchmarks for KV cache hit/miss scenarios - due 2026-04-12
Priya Nair: export workload replay traces and sample requests - due 2026-04-10
Luis Ortega: draft updated incident runbook and postmortem doc (v0) - due 2026-04-16
transcript:
[00:00] Michael (Redwood AE): Hey everyone, thanks for joining. I think we have about 55 minutes, we'll run through the timeline quickly then talk mitigations and next steps. Tom, do you want to kick off with the customer side summary?
[00:12] Tom (Verdant CTO): Yeah sure, sorry for the late follow-up. So on Friday we saw a big spike in tail latency around 02:10 UTC, a number of in-flight requests hit p99/p999 and a bunch of retries kicked in. It looks like the Dedicated pool autoscaler failed to absorb sudden concurrency.
[00:31] Priya (SRE): quick note, some of the log names are a bit off in our dashboard, it's mixing up the model variants, so we were, uh, chasing the wrong node for about 12 minutes.
[00:40] Sana (Redwood SE): okay, that aligns with what we saw. Initial signs pointed to a KV cache thrash; the prefix cache got invalidated during a spike and a lot of long sequence requests warmed cold caches which drove GPU utilization up and increased latency.
[00:57] Evan (Security): Were any requests re-routed to the hosted service? We need to confirm no customer data left the VPC during rollback.
[01:05] Michael: short answer: no. All traffic stayed in Verdant's Dedicated cluster. We did not failover to hosted. We did enable degraded-mode routing temporarily for lower tier routes but that was within the same private deployment.
[01:20] Jamal (Ops): And the autoscaler — it launched new nodes but they came up in a different instance type, which had a different kernel scheduling profile; that mismatch increased cold-start token time.
[01:33] Sana: yep, that was the other piece — autoscaler backfilled from a pool with mixed GPU kernels. Our runtime depends on steady kernel selection for latencies < 50ms; when it switches kernels mid-stream you see tail effects.
[01:47] Tom: so root cause hypothesis is basically twofold: cache thrash + autoscaler introduced heterogenous kernels. Any disagreement?
[01:55] Michael: that sounds right. Our postmortem analysis shows a pattern where prefix cache invalidation coincided with a sudden surge of long-seq requests hitting a single partition. The autoscaler policy allowed cross-pool fills which introduced a different optimized kernel rotor.
[02:12] Priya: we had some config we inherited from previous infra, the metric threshold for scale-up was a moving average which smoothed the spike; by the time it added nodes it's... it's too late.
[02:26] Sana: short-term fixes we've pushed: 1) tightened autoscaler rules to prefer same-kernel instance types, 2) increased prefix cache retention for the hot partition, 3) temporarily limited max seq length for non-critical routes to reduce cache pressure.
[02:42] Michael: We also rolled a quick patch that prevents cross-pool kernel switching during active batches. It's a short-lived guard to avoid mixing runtime kernels mid-request.
[02:52] Tom: saw that, thanks. Any security concerns from enabling that guard?
[02:58] Evan: nothing major; we reviewed the guard, it doesn't change data flows. Need to capture audit logs and token-level access for the change just to be safe.
[03:08] Michael: logs were captured. We'll include the RBAC events and KMS key use in the follow-up bundle.
[03:16] Priya: a question on KV cache: is the cache global or per-shard? We heard different things in the heatmap.
[03:23] Sana: per-shard. But on this workload the shard mapping skewed so many hot prefixes landed on one shard. We're proposing two options — redistribute hot prefixes or add shard-aware cache replication. Both have tradeoffs.
[03:37] Maya (Product): for us, reliability for checkout routes is higher priority than cost. If replication buys lower p999 we prefer that.
[03:45] Michael: note taken. We'll model the cost impact.
[03:49] Jamal: any immediate rollback plan if this reoccurs?
[03:52] Michael: we have a canary autoscaler rule to roll back to prior pool and to pin kernel types. If we see tail degrade past threshold, it will stop new allocations and route to pinned nodes only.
[04:05] Tom: can that be automated? manual toggle cost us 8 minutes last time.
[04:08] Sana: yes, automation possible. We're proposing an automated canary that runs on the median latency and kernel homogeneity check before permitting scale actions.
[04:18] Priya: one more — we need the raw p99 and p999 logs with timestamps correlated to autoscaler events.
[04:24] Michael: we'll share those. Expect a bundle with histograms, hvac — sorry, timestamped traces, and the autoscaler snapshots.
[04:33] Evan: regarding compliance: do we need any special attestations? SOC 2 was mentioned in the initial escalation, Verdant wants the audit trail.
[04:40] Michael: we'll include the audit logs and KMS key access records. Also we can provide the SOC 2 cert and PCI scope notes that apply to Dedicated deployments.
[04:52] Tom: next steps and owners?
[04:55] Michael: I'll upload logs and a first-pass timeline by 2026-04-09. Sana will run microbenchmarks by 2026-04-12. Luis will draft runbook updates v0 by 2026-04-16. Verdant provides workload replay and critical routes by 2026-04-10. We'll schedule a deeper kernel/quant benchmark the week of 2026-04-13.
[05:18] Maya: also please include cost delta estimates for shard replication vs redistribution. We need to justify to finance.
[05:25] Michael: will do.
[05:29] Tom: thanks everyone. Appreciate the quick action. We'll reconvene after the artifacts are shared.
[05:35] Michael: thanks, end call.
notes: Transcript contains occasional transcription artifacts (e.g., 'hvac' mis-transcription of 'timestamped traces'), speaker interruptions, and some mis-attributed short labels as typical of Fireflies exports.
